sources.entry: 2. Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE

summary.title: Secure Coding Guidelines for Java SE
summary.one_liner: Oracle's guideline document lists numbered secure coding rules for Java covering trust boundaries, least privilege, resource exhaustion (DoS), resource release, integer overflow, and exception handling.
takeaways: Establish trust boundaries and validate data crossing them; threat modeling helps identify these boundaries.
Run code with least privilege and isolate untrusted code in separate JVMs or processes, since the security manager is disabled.
Guard against resource exhaustion: limit decompressed sizes, XML entity expansion, image dimensions, and deserialization of untrusted data.
Always release resources (try-with-resources or try/finally) and prevent integer overflow in resource limit checks.
Do not use untrusted data as keys in HashMap/HashSet, and keep third-party libraries updated.
summary.summary: This Oracle document (version 11.0, June 2025) gives a set of security-focused coding guidelines for Java SE developers, extending general references such as Effective Java. It is organized as numbered guidelines (e.g., 0-0 through 0-8 on fundamentals, 1-1 through 1-4 on denial of service) that each explain a risk and recommended practice. Examples are shown in Java code, such as the Execute Around Method pattern, try-with-resources, overflow-safe checks with Math and Objects methods, and XML secure processing settings. The guidance is aimed at all Java developers and is not about implementing cryptography.
